claim: Viruses interact with hundreds to thousands of proteins in mammals.
source: Viruses interact with hundreds to thousands of proteins in mammals, yet adaptation against viruses has only been studied in a few proteins specialized in antiviral defense.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a foundational premise of the study.

claim: Adaptation against viruses has only been studied in a few proteins specialized in antiviral defense.
source: Viruses interact with hundreds to thousands of proteins in mammals, yet adaptation against viruses has only been studied in a few proteins specialized in antiviral defense.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by the introduction's discussion of limited known cases.

claim: Viruses use the more evolutionarily constrained proteins within the cellular functions they interact with.
source: We show that viruses (i) use the more evolutionarily constrained proteins within the cellular functions they interact with
evidence: This is a main finding stated in the abstract and supported by pN/pS analysis in the results.

claim: Despite high constraint, virus-interacting proteins account for a high proportion of all protein adaptation in humans and other mammals.
source: that (ii) despite this high constraint, virus-interacting proteins account for a high proportion of all protein adaptation in humans and other mammals.
evidence: This is a main finding stated in the abstract and supported by MK test and BS-REL test results.

claim: Adaptation is elevated in virus-interacting proteins across all functional categories, including both immune and non-immune functions.
source: Adaptation is elevated in virus-interacting proteins across all functional categories, including both immune and non-immune functions.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by GO analysis in the results.

claim: Viruses have driven close to 30% of all adaptive amino acid changes in the part of the human proteome conserved within mammals.
source: We conservatively estimate that viruses have driven close to 30% of all adaptive amino acid changes in the part of the human proteome conserved within mammals.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by the asymptotic MK test results showing α=27% in VIPs.

claim: Viruses are one of the most dominant drivers of evolutionary change across mammalian and human proteomes.
source: Our results suggest that viruses are one of the most dominant drivers of evolutionary change across mammalian and human proteomes.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract, based on the proportion of adaptive changes attributed to viruses.

claim: Protein kinase R (PKR) is one of the fastest adaptively evolving proteins in mammals.
source: PKR is one of the fastest adaptively evolving proteins in mammals.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an example of a well-known antiviral protein.

claim: Specific amino acid changes in PKR have been shown to be associated with an arms race against viral decoys for the control of translation.
source: Specific amino acid changes in PKR have been shown to be associated with an arms race against viral decoys for the control of translation (Elde et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to Elde et al., 2009.

claim: Most VIPs are not specialized in antiviral defense and do not have known roles in immunity.
source: Most VIPs are not specialized in antiviral defense and do not have known roles in immunity.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by the finding that only 5% of VIPs have known antiviral activity.

claim: Most VIPs evolve unusually slowly rather than unusually fast both in animals and in plants.
source: First, most VIPs evolve unusually slowly rather than unusually fast both in animals (Davis et al., 2015; Jäger et al., 2011) and in plants (Mukhtar et al., 2011; Weßling et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to multiple studies.

claim: VIPs tend to interact with proteins that are functionally important hubs in the protein-protein interaction network of the host.
source: Second, VIPs tend to interact with proteins that are functionally important hubs in the protein-protein interaction network of the host possibly limiting their ability to adapt (Dyer et al., 2008; Halehalli and Nagarajaram, 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: Very few cases of adaptation to viruses are known outside of fast evolving, specialized antiviral proteins.
source: Finally, very few cases of adaptation to viruses are known outside of fast evolving, specialized antiviral proteins (Demogines et al., 2012; Meyerson et al., 2014; Meyerson and Sawyer, 2011; Meyerson et al., 2015; Ng et al., 2015; Ortiz et al., 2009; Schaller et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: Transferrin receptor (TFRC) is the most notable exception of a non-immune, housekeeping protein that adapts in response to viruses.
source: Transferrin receptor or TFRC is the most notable exception, and serves as a striking example of a non-immune, housekeeping protein used by viruses (Demogines et al., 2013; Kaelber et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: TFRC is responsible for iron uptake in many different cell types and is used as a cell surface receptor by diverse viruses in rodents and carnivores.
source: TFRC is responsible for iron uptake in many different cell types and is used as a cell surface receptor by diverse viruses in rodents and carnivores.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction.

claim: TFRC has repeatedly evaded binding by viruses through recurrent adaptive amino acid changes.
source: TFRC has repeatedly evaded binding by viruses through recurrent adaptive amino acid changes.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction.

claim: The study analyzed ~1300 VIPs manually curated from a set of ~10000 proteins conserved across 24 well-sequenced mammalian genomes.
source: Here we analyze patterns of evolutionary constraint and adaptation in a high quality set of ~1300 VIPs that we manually curated from virology literature. These 1300 VIPs come from a set of ~10000 proteins conserved across 24 well-sequenced mammalian genomes (Materials and methods).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction describing the study design.

claim: The vast majority of VIPs (~80%) have no known antiviral or any other more broadly defined immune activity.
source: As expected, the vast majority of these VIPs (~80%) have no known antiviral or any other more broadly defined immune activity.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by data in Supplementary file 1D.

claim: VIPs do tend to evolve slowly.
source: We confirm that VIPs do tend to evolve slowly and demonstrate that this is because VIPs experience much stronger evolutionary constraint than other proteins within the same functional categories.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a finding confirmed by the study.

claim: VIPs experience much stronger evolutionary constraint than other proteins within the same functional categories.
source: We confirm that VIPs do tend to evolve slowly and demonstrate that this is because VIPs experience much stronger evolutionary constraint than other proteins within the same functional categories.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a finding of the study.

claim: Despite greater evolutionary constraint, VIPs display higher rates of adaptation compared to other proteins.
source: However, despite this greater evolutionary constraint, VIPs display higher rates of adaptation compared to other proteins.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a main finding.

claim: The excess of adaptation in VIPs is visible across biological functions, on multiple time scales, in multiple taxa, and across multiple studied viruses.
source: This excess of adaptation is visible in VIPs across biological functions, on multiple time scales, in multiple taxa, and across multiple studied viruses.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a summary of findings.

claim: The study curated a set of 1256 VIPs from the low-throughput virology literature.
source: We curated a set of 1256 VIPs from the low-throughput virology literature (Materials and methods and Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the dataset.

claim: VIPs were defined as proteins that interact physically with viral proteins, viral RNA, and/or viral DNA.
source: VIPs were defined as proteins that interact physically with viral proteins, viral RNA, and/or viral DNA (Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This is the operational definition used in the study.

claim: Interactions identified by high-throughput experiments were excluded because of concerns about a high rate of false positives.
source: We excluded interactions identified by high-throughput experiments because we were concerned about a high rate of false positives (Mellacheruvu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as a methodological choice with a citation.

claim: The 1256 VIPs were annotated from an initial set of 9861 proteins with clear orthologs in all 24 analyzed mammalian high quality genomes.
source: The 1256 VIPs were annotated from an initial set of 9861 proteins with clear orthologs in all 24 analyzed mammalian high quality genomes (Figure 1, Supplementary file 1B and Materials and methods) (Enard et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1.

claim: Most of the VIPs (95%) correspond to an interaction between a human protein and a virus infecting humans.
source: Most of the VIPs (95%) correspond to an interaction between a human protein and a virus infecting humans (Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to supplementary data.

claim: Human Immunodeficiency Virus type 1 (HIV-1) is the best-represented virus with 240 VIPs.
source: Human Immunodeficiency Virus type 1 (HIV-1) is the best-represented virus with 240 VIPs, with nine other viruses (HPV, HCV, EBV, HBV, HSV, Influenza Virus, ADV, HTLV and KSHV) having at least 50 VIPs (Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to supplementary data.

claim: Nine other viruses (HPV, HCV, EBV, HBV, HSV, Influenza Virus, ADV, HTLV and KSHV) have at least 50 VIPs.
source: Human Immunodeficiency Virus type 1 (HIV-1) is the best-represented virus with 240 VIPs, with nine other viruses (HPV, HCV, EBV, HBV, HSV, Influenza Virus, ADV, HTLV and KSHV) having at least 50 VIPs (Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to supplementary data.

claim: This dataset represents the largest, most up-to-date set of VIPs backed by individual low-throughput publications.
source: This dataset represents the largest, most up-to-date set of VIPs backed by individual low-throughput publications.
evidence: This is a claim about the dataset made in the Results section.

claim: Half of all publications reporting VIPs were published in the past 7 years.
source: Nonetheless, given that many VIPs were discovered only recently, with half of all publications reporting VIPs published in the past 7 years (Figure 2), it is likely that many additional VIPs remain to be discovered.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2.

claim: It is likely that many additional VIPs remain to be discovered.
source: Nonetheless, given that many VIPs were discovered only recently, with half of all publications reporting VIPs published in the past 7 years (Figure 2), it is likely that many additional VIPs remain to be discovered.
evidence: This is an inference based on the recent pace of discovery shown in Figure 2.

claim: The identified 1256 VIPs are involved in diverse cellular and supracellular processes with 162 overlapping GO cellular and supracellular processes having more than 50 VIPs.
source: The identified 1256 VIPs are involved in diverse cellular and supracellular processes with 162 overlapping GO cellular and supracellular processes having more than 50 VIPs (Gene Ontology (GO) classes (October 2013 version) (Ashburner et al., 2000; The Gene Ontology Consortium, 2015); Supplementary file 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to GO analysis.

claim: VIP cellular processes include transcription (354 VIPs), post-translational protein modification (224 VIPs), signal transduction (396 VIPs), apoptosis (185 VIPs), and transport (264 VIPs).
source: These cellular processes include transcription (354 VIPs), post-translational protein modification (224 VIPs), signal transduction (396 VIPs), apoptosis (185 VIPs), and transport (264 VIPs).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the functional diversity of VIPs.

claim: VIP supracellular processes notably include defense response (103 VIPs) and developmental processes (327 VIPs).
source: The supracellular processes notably include defense response (103 VIPs) and developmental processes (327 VIPs).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the functional diversity of VIPs.

claim: Only 57 VIPs or 5% of VIPs have known antiviral activity.
source: Only 57 VIPs or 5% of VIPs have known antiviral activity (Supplementary file 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to supplementary data.

claim: 241 VIPs (20% of VIPs) have known immune functions.
source: These 57 antiviral VIPs are part of a larger group of 241 VIPs (20% of VIPs) with known immune functions, defined here as any activity that modulates the immune response or involved in the development of the immune response (Materials and methods and Supplementary file 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to supplementary data.

claim: More than 80% of the VIPs have no known immune activity.
source: Most - more than 80% - of the VIPs have no known immune activity.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: VIPs have ~15% lower mammal-wide dN/dS ratio compared to non-VIPs (0.124 versus 0.145).
source: On average, the VIPs have ~15% lower mammal-wide dN/dS ratio compared to non-VIPs (0.124 versus 0.145, 95% CI [0.136,0.148]; Materials and methods).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a measure of evolutionary rate.

claim: The difference in dN/dS between VIPs and non-VIPs is highly significant (permutation test P=0 after 10^9 iterations).
source: The difference in dN/dS is highly significant (permutation test P=0 after 109 iterations; Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a statistical result.

claim: In human African populations from the 1000 Genomes project, the average pN/pS is 21% lower in VIPs compared to non-VIPs (0.759 versus 0.966).
source: In the human African populations from the 1000 Genomes project (Materials and methods), the average pN/pS is 21% lower in VIPs compared to non-VIPs (0.759 versus 0.966, 95% CI [0.92,1.01], simple permutation test P=0 after 109 iterations).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a measure of purifying selection.

claim: VIPs show an excess of low frequency (≤10%) deleterious non-synonymous variants compared to non-VIPs.
source: VIPs also show an excess of low frequency (≤10%) deleterious non-synonymous variants compared to non-VIPs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; simple permutation test P=0 after 109 iterations).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: In great apes, the average pN/pS ratio is 25% lower in VIPs compared to non-VIPs (0.526 versus 0.697).
source: In great apes, the average pN/pS ratio is 25% lower in VIPs compared to non-VIPs (0.526 versus 0.697, 95% CI [0.66,0.72], simple permutation test P=0 after 109 iterations; Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Stronger purifying selection acting on VIPs is widespread and is not limited to VIPs interacting with any one particular virus.
source: Finally, stronger purifying selection acting on VIPs is widespread and is not limited to VIPs interacting with any one particular virus (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: VIPs are expressed in more tissues than non-VIPs both at the RNA level (25.5 tissues on average in VIPs versus 11.9 tissues in non-VIPs) and at the protein level (15.1 tissues on average for VIPs versus 6.1 for non-VIPs).
source: We confirm that VIPs are indeed expressed in more tissues than non-VIPs both at the RNA level (GTEx Consortium, 2015) (GTEx V4 RNA-seq expression RPKM≥10 in 25.5 tissues on average in VIPs versus 11.9 tissues in non-VIPs, simple permutation test P=0) and at the protein level (Kim et al., 2014) (Human Proteome Map spectral count≥5 in 15.1 tissues on average for VIPs versus 6.1 for non-VIPs, simple permutation test P=0).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to expression data sources.

claim: VIPs have many more protein-protein interaction partners than non-VIPs (18.4 on average versus 3.2).
source: VIPs also have many more protein-protein interaction partners than non-VIPs based on a dataset of human protein-protein interactions curated by (Luisi et al., 2015) from the Biogrid database (Stark et al., 2011) (18.4 on average versus 3.2, simple permutation test P=0).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to interaction data sources.

claim: The difference in pN/pS between VIPs and non-VIPs is driven at least partly by the fact that VIPs tend to be hubs with many interacting partners in the human protein-protein interactions network.
source: These results show that VIPs do experience stronger purifying selection than non-VIPs, and that the difference in purifying selection is driven at least partly by the fact that VIPs tend to be hubs with many interacting partners in the human protein-protein interactions network.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the data.

claim: Within a wide range of host functions, viruses tend to interact with the most conserved proteins.
source: This shows that within a wide range of host functions, viruses tend to interact with the most conserved proteins.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from GO-matched analysis.

claim: Immune VIPs have a significantly reduced pN/pS ratio compared to immune non-VIPs.
source: Interestingly, even immune VIPs (Supplementary file 1D) have a significantly reduced pN/pS ratio compared to immune non-VIPs (Figure 3C), which suggests that immune proteins in direct physical contact with viruses are more constrained.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The reduction in pN/pS in non-immune VIPs is very similar to the reduction observed in the entire set of VIPs.
source: The reduction in pN/pS in non-immune VIPs is very similar to the reduction observed in the entire set of VIPs (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Using the classic MK test with variants with derived allele frequency ≥10%, α is strongly elevated in VIPs compared to non-VIPs (α=0.19 in VIPs versus −0.02 in non-VIPs, permutation test P=2.x10−5).
source: We find that α is strongly elevated in VIPs compared to non-VIPs (α=0.19 in VIPs versus −0.02 in non-VIPs, permutation test P=2.x10−5).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a result of the classic MK test.

claim: The difference in α between VIPs and non-VIPs is robust to recombination, coding sequence GC content, coding sequence length, expression levels, and number of protein-protein interactions.
source: The difference in α is robust to recombination (α =−0.025 in non-VIPs with similar recombination to VIPs versus −0.02 without control). It is also robust to coding sequence GC content (α=−0.019 with versus −0.02 without control), coding sequence length (α=−0.023 with versus −0.02 without control). The difference is also robust to variation in levels of expression at the RNA level measured as the number of tissues with GTEx V4 RNA-seq expression RPKM≥10 (α=0.001 with versus 0.02 without control) and as the average expression across all GTEx V4 tissues (α=−0.018 with versus 0.02 without control), as well as at the protein level measured as the number of Human Proteome Map tissues with spectral count>=5 (α=−0.024 with versus 0.02 without control) or the average expression across all the Human Proteome Map tissues (α=−0.035 with versus 0.02 without control). The difference in α is also not affected by the number of protein-protein interactions (α=0.025 with versus −0.02 without control).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as robustness checks for the MK test results.

claim: The higher rate of adaptation in VIPs is not explained by higher rates of adaptation in the host GO processes where VIPs are well represented (α=0.003 with versus −0.02 without control).
source: Finally, we match VIPs and non-VIPs with similar GO categories (Materials and methods, paragraph titled 'Gene Ontology-matching control samples'). The higher rate of adaptation in VIPs is not explained by higher rates of adaptation in the host GO processes where VIPs are well represented (α=0.003 with versus −0.02 without control).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a result of GO-matched analysis.

claim: The excess of adaptation in VIPs is robust to many different host factors.
source: Together these results show that the excess of adaptation in VIPs is robust to many different host factors.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from robustness checks.

claim: HIV-1 and Hepatitis B Virus (HBV) VIPs display statistically significant increases in adaptation.
source: Although the small number of proteins interacting with individual viruses precludes precise estimates of α (see the large confidence intervals on Figure 4A), the VIPs show nominally higher values of α for eight out of 10 viruses, with HIV-1 and Hepatitis B Virus (HBV) displaying statistically significant increases in adaptation.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: VIPs in most GO categories show higher rates of adaptation (14 out of 20) with 9 of 14 showing statistically significant increases.
source: Likewise, VIPs in most GO categories show higher rates of adaptation (14 out of 20) with 9 of 14 showing statistically significant increases (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The 80% of VIPs with no known antiviral or broader immune function have a strongly increased rate of adaptation according to the classic MK test (α=0.26 in VIPs versus 0.02 in non-VIPs, permutation test P=3x10−7).
source: Finally and importantly, the 80% of VIPs with no known antiviral or broader immune function (Supplementary file 1D) have a strongly increased rate of adaptation according to the classic MK test (α=0.26 in VIPs versus 0.02 in non-VIPs, permutation test P=3x10−7; Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Immune VIPs, including antiviral VIPs, do not show any increase of adaptation compared to immune non-VIPs.
source: Intriguingly, unlike for non-immune VIPs or all VIPs considered together (top of Figure 4B), immune VIPs, including antiviral VIPs (Supplementary file 1D), do not show any increase of adaptation compared to immune non-VIPs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The asymptotic MK test estimate of α in VIPs is 27% (512 out of 1897 amino acid changes) compared to ~9% (1293 out of 14,370 amino acid changes) in non-VIPs.
source: The asymptotic MK test estimate of α in VIPs is 27% (512 out of 1897 amino acid changes) compared to ~9% (1293 out of 14,370 amino acid changes) in non-VIPs (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Although VIPs represent only 13% of the orthologs in the dataset and only 11% of all amino acid substitutions, they account for almost 30% of all adaptive amino-acid changes in human evolution.
source: Thus, although VIPs represent only 13% of the orthologs in our dataset and only 11% of all amino acid substitutions, we estimate that in human evolution they account for almost 30% of all adaptive amino-acid changes.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the asymptotic MK test.

claim: VIPs have experienced twice as many adaptive amino acid changes on average compared to non-VIPs across mammals.
source: We estimate that all VIPs have experienced twice as many adaptive amino acid changes on average compared to non-VIPs (Figure 5A, permutation test P=0 after 109 iterations).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: VIPs with the strongest evidence of adaptation (BUSTED P-values lower than 10-5) have a six-fold excess of strong signals of adaptation.
source: Figure 5A shows that VIPs with the strongest evidence of adaptation (BUSTED P-values lower than 10-5) have a six-fold excess of strong signals of adaptation (permutation test P=0 after 109 permutations).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The excess of adaptation in VIPs is due to more VIPs with signals of adaptation than non-VIPs, more branches of the tree per VIP showing adaptation, and a greater proportion of codons evolving adaptively per branch.
source: In Figure 5—figure supplement 3 we further show that this excess of adaptation in VIPs is due to i) more VIPs with signals of adaptation than non-VIPs, ii) more branches of the tree per VIP showing adaptation, and iii) a greater proportion of codons evolving adaptively per branch.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Nine out of the ten viruses with more than 50 VIPs show a strong excess of adaptation in their respective VIPs.
source: Nine out of the ten viruses show a strong excess of adaptation in their respective VIPs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing virus-specific analysis.

claim: HIV-1 and HBV VIPs have the strongest excess of adaptation, with three times as many selected codons as non-VIPs.
source: HIV-1 and HBV VIPs have the strongest excess, with three times as many selected codons as non-VIPs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing virus-specific analysis.

claim: HCV has no known close viral relatives despite extensive screening of diverse mammalian species.
source: As mentioned above, HCV stands out among the ten viruses with the largest number of VIPs in humans in that it has no known close viral relatives despite extensive screening of diverse mammalian species (Quan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation.

claim: The 109 VIPs of HCV are the only ones where no excess of adaptation is detected along the mammalian tree.
source: In line with this prediction, the 109 VIPs of HCV are the only ones where we do not detect any excess of adaptation along the mammalian tree (Figure 5B) despite being one of the largest groups of VIPs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Of 162 GO categories with more than 50 VIPs, 118 (73%) have a 50% or greater excess of adaptation in VIPs.
source: Of these 162 GO categories, 118 (73%) have a 50% or greater excess of adaptation in VIPs (Supplementary file 1C, permutation test p<0.05 in all cases).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing GO analysis.

claim: The excess of adaptation in VIPs is widespread across host functions.
source: The excess of adaptation in VIPs is therefore widespread across host functions.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from GO analysis.

claim: Immune VIPs have a very strong excess of adaptation compared to immune non-VIPs.
source: As expected, immune VIPs have a very strong excess of adaptation compared to immune non-VIPs (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5C.

claim: VIPs with no known immune function show a very similar excess of adaptation compared to all VIPs.
source: Importantly, VIPs with no known immune function (Supplementary file 1D) show a very similar excess of adaptation compared to all VIPs (Figure 5A, black versus grey lines; permutation test P=0 after 109 iterations).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: All mammalian clades in the tree show a similar excess of adaptation in VIPs.
source: However, all mammalian clades in the tree show a similar excess of adaptation in VIPs (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Primates stand out due to their low overall proportions of positively selected codons compared to the other mammalian clades in the tree.
source: Primates stand out due to their low overall proportions of positively selected codons compared to the other mammalian clades in the tree (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The low proportion of positively selected codons in primates is most likely due to a lower statistical power of the BS-REL test in the short primate branches.
source: This is most likely due to a lower statistical power of the BS-REL test in the short primate branches (Kosakovsky Pond et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation with a citation.

claim: VIPs with strong signals of adaptation show such signals in all the mammalian clades represented.
source: In line with this, VIPs with strong signals of adaptation show such signals in all the mammalian clades represented (Figure 6).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6.

claim: Phylogenetically widespread excess of recurrent adaptation suggests that many of the VIPs annotated in humans were also VIPs for a substantial evolutionary time in a wide range of mammals.
source: This phylogenetically widespread excess of recurrent adaptation suggests that many of the VIPs annotated in humans were also VIPs for a substantial evolutionary time in a wide range of mammals.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the phylogenetic distribution of adaptation.

claim: Aminopeptidase N (ANPEP) is the most positively selected non-antiviral VIP that fulfills requirements for in-depth investigation.
source: The most positively selected non-antiviral VIP that fulfills all these requirements is aminopeptidase N, abbreviated ANPEP, APN or CD13 (Mina-Osorio, 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the case study selection.

claim: Analysis of a phylogenetic tree including 84 mammals confirms pervasive adaptation of ANPEP across mammals, with 76 out of 165 branches in the tree showing signals of adaptation.
source: The analysis of a phylogenetic tree including 84 mammals (Supplementary file 1J) confirms pervasive adaptation of ANPEP across mammals, with 76 out of 165 branches in the tree showing signals of adaptation (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Adaptation of ANPEP has previously been detected in the context of oxidative stress in Cetaceans.
source: Note that adaptation of ANPEP has previously been detected in the context of oxidative stress in Cetaceans (Yim et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation.

claim: ANPEP is a cell-surface enzyme well known for its surprisingly wide range and diversity of functions.
source: ANPEP is a cell-surface enzyme well known for its surprisingly wide range and diversity of functions (Mina-Osorio, 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation.

claim: ANPEP is used by group I coronaviruses as a receptor, including HCoV-229E, TGEV, FCoV, CCoV, PRCV and PEDV.
source: In particular, it is used by group I coronaviruses as a receptor, including the Human Coronavirus 229E (HCoV-229E) (Yeager et al., 1992), Transmissible Gastroenteritis Virus (TGEV) (Delmas et al., 1992), Feline Coronavirus (FCoV) (Tresnan and Holmes, 1998), Canine Coronavirus (CCoV) (Tusell et al., 2007), Porcine Respiratory Coronavirus (PRCV) (Delmas et al., 1993) and Porcine Epidemic Diarrhea Virus (PEDV) (Oh et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with multiple citations.

claim: Reguera et al. solved the structure of porcine ANPEP bound together with TGEV and PRCV.
source: Reguera et al. (Reguera et al., 2012) solved the structure of porcine ANPEP bound together with TGEV and PRCV.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation.

claim: Reguera et al. identified 22 amino acids in the extracellular domain of ANPEP that form a surface of contact with TGEV and PRCV.
source: The authors identified in the extracellular domain of ANPEP 22 amino acids that form a surface of contact with TGEV and PRCV (Figure 7B) (Pettersen et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations and shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The most important component of the ANPEP contact surface for host tropism is a N-glycosylation site at position 736 in porcine ANPEP (orthologous position 739 in human ANPEP) that forms hydrogen bonds with TGEV and PRCV.
source: The most important component of this contact surface for host tropism is a N-glycosylation site at position 736 in porcine ANPEP (orthologous position 739 in human ANPEP) that forms hydrogen bonds with TGEV and PRCV (Tusell et al., 2007; Reguera et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations.

claim: Deleting the N-glycosylation site at position 736 abolishes the ability of TGEV and PRCV to bind porcine ANPEP.
source: Deleting this site abolishes the ability of TGEV and PRCV to bind porcine ANPEP (Reguera et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation.

claim: Adding the N-glycosylation site in human ANPEP that natively lacks it transforms it into a receptor for TGEV and PRCV.
source: Adding the glycosylation site in human ANPEP that natively lacks it transforms it into a receptor for TGEV and PRCV (Reguera et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation.

claim: MEME test detects significant adaptation (MEME p≤0.05) in 85 of the 931 aligned codons in ANPEP.
source: We use the MEME test from HYPHY (Murrell et al., 2012) to identify codons in ANPEP that were under episodic adaptive evolution in mammals. MEME detects significant adaptation (MEME p≤0.05) in 85 of the 931 aligned codons.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a result of the MEME test.

claim: Several adaptively evolving codons in ANPEP are within, or right next to the surface of contact with TGEV and PRCV.
source: Interestingly, several of these adaptively evolving codons are within, or right next to the surface of contact with TGEV and PRCV (Figure 7B and C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7B and C.

claim: The codons in contact with TGEV and PRCV and their neighbors are strongly enriched in adaptation compared to ANPEP codons as a whole.
source: The codons in contact with TGEV and PRCV and their neighbors are strongly enriched in adaptation compared to ANPEP codons as a whole (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7C.

claim: This enrichment in adaptation fades very rapidly as one gets further from the surface of contact with TGEV and PRCV.
source: This enrichment fades very rapidly as one gets further from the surface of contact with TGEV and PRCV, consistent with detected adaptation being related to interaction with coronaviruses, and not to a more diffuse, less specific enrichment within a wider segment of ANPEP (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Two codons within the consensus motif for the N-glycosylation site responsible for host tropism evolved adaptively in mammals (MEME P=0.005 for both).
source: Adaptively evolving codons in the contact surface with TGEV and PRCV most notably include two codons within the consensus motif for the N-glycosylation site responsible for host tropism (Figure 7B). N-glycosylation is governed by a three amino acids consensus, NX[ST], where X can be anything except proline (Bause, 1983). The first and third positions in the consensus evolved adaptively in mammals (MEME P=0.005 for both).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The mammalian ancestor had a fully functional consensus for N-glycosylation at the relevant site in ANPEP.
source: The ancestral states of the two positions shows that the mammalian ancestor had a fully functional consensus for N-glycosylation, and that the consensus was lost independently 11 times in mammals, either by modification of the first or third position (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The N-glycosylation consensus was lost independently 11 times in mammals.
source: The ancestral states of the two positions shows that the mammalian ancestor had a fully functional consensus for N-glycosylation, and that the consensus was lost independently 11 times in mammals, either by modification of the first or third position (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The N-glycosylation consensus was regained only two times after loss.
source: The consensus was regained only two times after loss (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The signals of adaptation detected at the first and third positions in the N-glycosylation consensus mainly reflect parallel, adaptive losses of the N-glycosylation site in multiple mammalian lineages.
source: This suggests that the signals of adaptation detected at the first and third positions in the consensus mainly reflect parallel, adaptive losses of the N-glycosylation site in multiple mammalian lineages.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the data.

claim: It is probable that the parallel adaptive losses of the N-glycosylation site in ANPEP were due to selective pressure exerted by ancient coronaviruses.
source: Given the crucial role of this N-glycosylation site in the binding of TGEV, PRCV, FCoV and CCoV to ANPEP, it is probable that these parallel adaptive losses were due to selective pressure exerted by ancient coronaviruses.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the data.

claim: Viruses have been a major selective pressure in the evolution of the mammalian proteome.
source: Here, we have shown that viruses have been a major selective pressure in the evolution of the mammalian proteome.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a main conclusion.

claim: Viruses appear to drive ~30% of all adaptive amino acid changes in the conserved part of the human proteome, as evidenced by the MK test.
source: Indeed viruses appear to drive ~30% of all adaptive amino acid changes in the conserved part of the human proteome, as evidenced by the MK test.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a main finding.

claim: The footprints of the arms race with viruses are visible in a large number of VIPs, and in a broad range of mammals.
source: Furthermore, the footprints of the arms race with viruses are visible in a large number of VIPs, and in a broad range of mammals.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a main finding.

claim: There is a substantial enrichment in strong signals of adaptation in VIPs with no known antiviral or other immune functions.
source: Importantly, we find a substantial enrichment in strong signals of adaptation in VIPs with no known antiviral or other immune functions (Figures 4B and 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a main finding.

claim: Adaptation to viruses is visible in VIPs with a very diverse range of functions including such core functions as transcription or signal transduction.
source: Instead adaptation to viruses is visible in VIPs with a very diverse range of functions including such core functions as transcription or signal transduction (Figures 4B, 5C and Supplementary file 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a main finding.

claim: This very diverse range of functions strongly argues in favor of a pervasive, external selective pressure –in our case viruses– as the cause for the observed signals.
source: This very diverse range of functions strongly argues in favor of a pervasive, external selective pressure –in our case viruses– as the cause for the observed signals.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an interpretation.

claim: Adaptation against viruses involves not only the specialized antiviral response, but also the entire population of host proteins that come into contact with viruses.
source: Our results thus draw a broader picture where adaptation against viruses involves not only the specialized antiviral response, but also the entire population of host proteins that come into contact with viruses.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a main conclusion.

claim: The transferrin receptor may represent the rule more than an exception for housekeeping proteins adapting in response to viruses.
source: The best-known case of a housekeeping protein having adapted in response to viruses, the transferrin receptor, may thus represent the rule more than an exception (Demogines et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an interpretation.

claim: NPC1 has very recently been shown to adapt against its use as a receptor by filoviruses in bats.
source: In line with this, a new non-antiviral protein, NPC1, has very recently been shown to adapt against its use as a receptor by filoviruses in bats (Ng et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a citation.

claim: The amount of adaptive evolution that can be attributed to viruses is probably underestimated by this analysis.
source: Although we find a strong signal of increased adaptation, the amount of adaptive evolution that can be attributed to viruses is probably underestimated by our analysis.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an interpretation.

claim: There are likely to be many undiscovered VIPs.
source: First, there likely to be many undiscovered VIPs.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a reason for underestimation.

claim: There is no sign that the pace of discovery of new VIPs is slowing down.
source: There is no sign that the pace of discovery of new VIPs is slowing down (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with reference to Figure 2.

claim: A substantial number of proteins classified as non-VIPs in this analysis are in fact VIPs, making non-VIPs a conservative control.
source: This means that a substantial number of proteins classified as non-VIPs in this analysis are in fact VIPs, making non-VIPs a conservative control.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a reason for underestimation.

claim: Adaptation in response to viruses is most likely not restricted to proteins that physically interact with viruses.
source: Second, adaptation in response to viruses is most likely not restricted to proteins that physically interact with viruses.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a reason for underestimation.

claim: Adaptation to viruses might happen in proteins that act downstream of VIPs in signaling cascades, or in non-coding sequences that regulate the expression of VIPs.
source: For example, adaptation to viruses might happen in proteins that act downstream of VIPs in signaling cascades, or in non-coding sequences that regulate the expression of VIPs.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a speculation.

claim: Not all of the 1256 VIPs used in the study have been consistently interacting with viruses during evolution.
source: Third, not all of the 1256 VIPs we use here have been consistently interacting with viruses during evolution.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a reason for underestimation.

claim: Most VIPs in the dataset (95%) were discovered in humans, and how frequently these VIPs have also been interacting with viruses in other mammals is currently unknown.
source: Most VIPs in the dataset (95%) were discovered in humans, and how frequently these VIPs have also been interacting with viruses in other mammals is currently unknown.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a limitation.

claim: The bias of the sample towards present human VIPs makes the results conservative.
source: Altogether, the bias of our sample towards present human VIPs thus makes our results conservative.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an interpretation.

claim: The results might explain why rates of protein adaptation appear relatively invariant across different biological functions assessed using GO analysis.
source: We speculate that our results might explain a puzzling observation that rates of protein adaptation appear relatively invariant across different biological functions assessed using GO analysis (Bierne and Eyre-Walker, 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a speculation with a citation.

claim: Because viruses (and likely other pathogens) interact with diverse proteins across most GO functions, they elevate the rate of adaptation across the whole proteome in a way that appears independent of specific functions in the GO analysis.
source: Because viruses (and likely other pathogens) interact with diverse proteins across most GO functions, they elevate the rate of adaptation across the whole proteome in a way that appears independent of specific functions in the GO analysis.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a speculation.

claim: Grouping genes together based on the way they interact with diverse pathogens or other environmental stimuli might be a profitable way for discerning the nature of selective pressures that have molded animal genomes.
source: We argue that grouping genes together based on the way they interact with diverse pathogens or other environmental stimuli might be a profitable way for discerning the nature of selective pressures that have molded animal genomes.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a suggestion.

claim: Viruses have exerted a very powerful selective pressure across the breadth of the mammalian proteome.
source: In conclusion, our analysis suggests that viruses have exerted a very powerful selective pressure across the breadth of the mammalian proteome, and suggests the possibility that pathogens in general are the key driver of protein adaptation in mammals and likely other lineages and might have driven many pleiotropic effects on diverse biological functions.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a main conclusion.

claim: Pathogens in general are possibly the key driver of protein adaptation in mammals and likely other lineages.
source: In conclusion, our analysis suggests that viruses have exerted a very powerful selective pressure across the breadth of the mammalian proteome, and suggests the possibility that pathogens in general are the key driver of protein adaptation in mammals and likely other lineages and might have driven many pleiotropic effects on diverse biological functions.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a speculation.
